subject: Archaeology
title: Ground-Penetrating Radar
description: A fast breakdown of Ground-Penetrating Radar for builders.

hook.text: A device on wheels can scan beneath the ground and find buried walls, tombs, and roads without digging.

buildup.text: Ground-penetrating radar sends radio waves into the earth. Different materials reflect the signal differently.

discovery.text: In 2020, GPR revealed a complete Viking ship burial under a farm in Norway — the first found in over a century.

twist.text: GPR works best in dry, sandy soil. Wet clay absorbs the signal, making many European sites difficult to scan.

climax.text: GPR mapped the entire Roman city of Falerii Novi without any excavation — streets, a market, a bath, and a temple.

punchline.text: We mapped a whole Roman city without moving a single stone.

quiz.question: What was mapped entirely by GPR without any excavation?
options: A complete Roman city called Falerii Novi
The tomb of Alexander the Great in Egypt
A lost Viking settlement in Iceland

details.summary: Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) sends radio waves into the earth and measures reflections from buried features — walls, floors, graves, ditches — creating subsurface maps without digging. It allows archaeologists to plan excavations by seeing what lies underground before breaking ground.
details.whyItMatters: GPR saves time and money by identifying buried features before excavation begins. It also locates sensitive features like graves without disturbing them, which is crucial for respectful treatment of human remains.
takeaways: Sends radio waves underground and maps reflected signals
Reveals buried walls, floors, graves, and other features
Allows site mapping without any excavation or ground disturbance

faq.question: How deep can ground-penetrating radar see?
faq.answer: Depth depends on soil type and antenna frequency. In dry sandy soil, GPR can detect features several meters deep. In wet clay, penetration is limited to under a meter. Higher frequencies give better resolution but shallower depth. Most archaeological surveys penetrate 1-3 meters.

faq.question: What was the most notable recent use of GPR in archaeology?
faq.answer: GPR surveys at former residential schools in Canada detected hundreds of potential unmarked graves, prompting national reckoning with indigenous boarding school history. In Italy, GPR mapped an entire Roman city at Falerii Novi without excavating, revealing streets and buildings underground.
